newsitem.title: USA: CRP may shift to Midwest from Plains - US analysts.
newsitem.headline: CRP may shift to Midwest from Plains - US analysts.

text.p: The U.S. Midwest may expand its presence in the Conservation Reserve and the Plains would lose its prominence under rules to be announced Wednesday by the U.S. Agriculture Department, analysts said.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman was scheduled to unveil the proposed rules during a news conference at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. The rules would be subject to a 45-day comment period.
"Congress did some restructuring of the CRP...We will honor that restructuring," Glickman told reporters during an impromptu meeting on Tuesday.
He declined to guess how much land would return to crops.

Glickman said the news conference would release "general guidelines on future operation" of CRP, the largest long-term land retirement program in U.S. history. He said there would be "enough detail" for farmers to know what land would qualify for the program and to judge rental rates.

Some 36.4 million acres of land were enrolled in the CRP, including 10.8 million acres with a history of wheat production, 4.3 million that used to grow corn and four million that went to soybeans in the past.
As part of the 1996 farm policy law, Congress put greater emphasis on water purity and wildlife habitat.
In addition, Congress allowed partial-field enrollments and continuous enrollment of land for filterstrips, grass waterways, windbreaks and wellhead protection areas.
All those initiatives, analysts said, would make the program more attractive to Midwestern land.
But there will be countervailing pressure, thanks to high soybean and feed grain prices, to keep Midwestern acreage in crop production, according to analysts.
"There will be some shift but I don't think it's going to be nearly as dramatic as some people have suggested," said Tim Warman of the conservation group American Farmland Trust.

Warman said he expected a "churning" of enrollment that would keep enrollment near the 36.4 million-acre ceiling but would bring out land that would not meet the environmental benefits index that would be applied by USDA.
There has been criticism that up to one-third of CRP land was not highly erodible. CRP was created in 1985 to give farmers an annual payment in exchange for idling fragile land for 10 years.
CRP revisions include an "early out" option allowing farmers to withdraw land from the reserve after 60 days' notice to USDA. Little land has been taken, however.
At the end of July, about 606,000 acres had been withdrawn under the early-out option.

Brian Willot, of the Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute at the University of Missouri, says environmental considerations could shift CRP acreage toward the Midwest and away from the Great Plains. He also noted that CRP enrollment would drop to 28 million acres by 2002, according to USDA estimates.
Some analysts have said farmers were disinclined to exercise the early-out option until they learned if they could re-enroll their land and if rental rates would be attractive.
